phases.title: Reality before syntax
phases.summary: Learners model business facts, identifiers, relationships, and ambiguity before writing SQL.
goals: Separate entities, attributes, events, and derived facts.
Identify ownership boundaries and unclear requirements before choosing tables.
Explain why a data model should preserve truth before it optimizes convenience.
exit_competencies: Can turn a short domain brief into candidate entities, identifiers, and relationships without using SQL syntax.
Can spot at least three ambiguous requirements that would change a schema design.
Can critique a paper model for duplicated facts, unclear ownership, and missing lifecycle events.

phases.title: SQL literacy basics
phases.summary: Learners read, filter, sort, insert, update, and delete rows in small known tables.
goals: Use basic SQL to inspect and change rows deliberately.
Predict which rows a simple predicate will include or exclude.
Read PostgreSQL errors as feedback about names, types, and constraints.
exit_competencies: Can write a SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT and explain the row set it returns.
Can perform INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE in a lab table and verify the changed rows.
Can diagnose common name, type, and NULL mistakes from PostgreSQL error messages.

phases.title: Relational joins and aggregation
phases.summary: Learners combine related tables and summarize row sets without losing track of grain.
goals: Use primary and foreign keys to explain table relationships.
Choose INNER and OUTER joins based on the question being asked.
Group rows at the right grain and check aggregates for duplication.
exit_competencies: Can join two or more related tables and explain which relationship each join follows.
Can identify when an aggregate is wrong because the query grouped or joined at the wrong grain.
Can repair a query that drops needed rows by using the correct outer join and predicate placement.

phases.title: Schema design and database-enforced truth
phases.summary: Learners use constraints, normalization, and migrations to make PostgreSQL enforce business truth.
goals: Choose keys and constraints that match durable business rules.
Normalize repeated facts while preserving queryable workflows.
Plan small migrations that tighten truth without losing existing data.
exit_competencies: Can defend a primary-key choice and explain the tradeoff between surrogate and natural identifiers.
Can add NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and FOREIGN KEY constraints to enforce named business rules.
Can critique a schema for update anomalies and repair it with a migration plan.

phases.title: PostgreSQL data modeling
phases.summary: Learners choose PostgreSQL-specific data types when they make a model clearer and more enforceable.
goals: Represent time, identity, flexible attributes, ranges, and arrays with PostgreSQL-native types.
Distinguish a useful JSONB boundary from a model that hides relational truth.
Use range and exclusion thinking for availability and scheduling problems.
exit_competencies: Can choose between normalized columns, JSONB, arrays, and ranges for a concrete requirement.
Can explain time zone storage and display behavior well enough to avoid local-time bugs.
Can model availability or validity intervals and identify overlapping data that should be rejected.

phases.title: Expressive querying
phases.summary: Learners shape complex answers with CTEs, subqueries, window functions, views, and set operations.
goals: Break a complex question into readable query stages.
Use window functions without collapsing the underlying row set.
Choose views and materialized views only when the lifecycle is understood.
exit_competencies: Can use a CTE or subquery to make a complex transformation inspectable without changing semantics.
Can write ranking, running total, and peer-comparison queries with window functions.
Can critique whether a view or materialized view improves a workflow or hides ownership and refresh problems.

phases.title: Transactions, concurrency, and correctness
phases.summary: Learners reason about correctness when multiple sessions read and write the same data.
goals: Use transactions to group changes into atomic units.
Observe locking, blocking, deadlocks, and isolation effects in multiple sessions.
Select the least surprising correctness mechanism for a workload.
exit_competencies: Can reproduce a lost-update style bug and repair it with an appropriate transaction or locking pattern.
Can explain what another session can see under READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE.
Can diagnose a lock wait or deadlock from PostgreSQL observations and name the competing statements.

phases.title: Indexing and query plans
phases.summary: Learners connect query shape, planner estimates, access methods, and index maintenance cost.
goals: Read EXPLAIN output well enough to predict access paths and row flow.
Design B-tree, composite, partial, expression, GIN, GiST, and BRIN indexes for observed workloads.
Reject indexes that lack a clear query, selectivity, or maintenance justification.
exit_competencies: Can explain why a query uses a sequential scan, index scan, bitmap scan, or join strategy from an EXPLAIN plan.
Can explain why a query uses a partial index instead of a full index and predict which rows will be read.
Can evaluate the write, storage, bloat, and maintenance cost of adding an index.

phases.title: PostgreSQL full-text search
phases.summary: Learners build lexical search with PostgreSQL core before considering semantic or extension-heavy search.
goals: Convert text into searchable vectors and queries.
Rank, filter, and inspect search results with language-aware behavior.
Compare full-text search, trigram preview, and external search without skipping workload evidence.
exit_competencies: Can build a searchable tsvector column or expression and index it with GIN.
Can explain why a document matched a tsquery by inspecting lexemes and configuration behavior.
Can tune ranking and filtering for a concrete document-search workflow without reaching first for vector search.

phases.title: Partitioning and large-table operations
phases.summary: Learners use partitioning for demonstrated scale, retention, and maintenance needs rather than as a default.
goals: Recognize the workload signals that make partitioning worth its operational cost.
Design range, list, and hash partitioning around query and retention behavior.
Operate partitions through attach, detach, pruning, indexes, and maintenance windows.
exit_competencies: Can decide that partitioning is not yet justified when volume, retention, or query patterns do not support it.
Can design a range-partitioned event table and predict which partitions a filtered query should prune.
Can plan partition maintenance steps without blocking normal writes longer than the workload allows.

phases.title: Roles, RLS, replication concepts, and FDW
phases.summary: Learners reason about access boundaries, tenant isolation, data movement, and federation at a core-concepts level.
goals: Design roles and grants around application and operator responsibilities.
Use row-level security policies to enforce tenant boundaries in the database.
Explain replication and FDW concepts well enough to choose cautious next steps.
exit_competencies: Can create a least-privilege role model and explain which actor can perform each database action.
Can implement and test a row-level security policy that prevents cross-tenant reads and writes.
Can explain the difference between logical replication, physical replication, and FDW without treating any as a generic scaling fix.

domains.summary: Orders, customers, products, payments, fulfillment, and support data provide a familiar transactional workload for SQL, joins, constraints, indexing, and operational critique.
People, resources, availability, reservations, and conflicts make time, ranges, exclusion, concurrency, and critique concrete.
Tenants, users, memberships, accounts, and scoped business records provide recurring practice for ownership, isolation, roles, RLS, and capstone-scale design.
Append-heavy operational events, telemetry, audit records, and retention windows drive expressive querying, indexing, partitioning, and operational planning.
Articles, tickets, comments, metadata, corpora, and search sessions support JSONB boundaries, full-text search, ranking, and extension posture.
Legacy schemas, foreign systems, replication boundaries, and migration checkpoints support FDW, logical replication concepts, and cautious modernization plans.

capstones.title: Multi-tenant SaaS CRM
capstones.summary: Design, secure, query, and defend a tenant-scoped CRM with realistic reporting and access-control obligations.

capstones.title: Scheduling and availability
capstones.summary: Model availability, prevent conflicts, handle concurrent booking attempts, and explain the operational behavior.

capstones.title: Event-heavy operations
capstones.summary: Handle high-volume events with retention, indexing, partitioning, monitoring posture, and explicit extension justification.

capstones.title: Modernization bridge
capstones.summary: Bridge a legacy system into PostgreSQL using careful schema repair, FDW or replication concepts, and staged cutover reasoning.
